prompt: What does the passage establish about divine wisdom through the story of Solomon?

options.text: That it can be lost, since a time came when Solomon's wisdom was turned to foolishness
That it grows steadily throughout a wise man's life
That it passes to a man's children after him
That it is withdrawn only at death

explanation: The section is headed IT CAN BE LOST. The key word in Proverbs 3:18 is retaineth: happy is every one that RETAINETH her, which implies she can be let go.

why.a: Correct. Loss is the whole point of the section, and Solomon is the proof.
why.b: Wrong. Solomon's arc runs the other way, from wisest to most foolish.
why.c: Wrong. Inheritance of wisdom is never suggested; Chapter 4 says God is its only source.
why.d: Wrong. Solomon lost it while alive, which is what makes the warning urgent.

prompt: Which statement of Solomon's shows that he had lost his wisdom?

options.text: "For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow"
"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom"
"I communed with mine own heart"
"Happy is the man that findeth wisdom"

explanation: Ecclesiastes 1:18. His joy was gone, and the lament that follows is 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity', which the author glosses as asking what the benefit of life is.

why.a: Correct. Ecclesiastes 1:18 is the evidence of loss, since wisdom is supposed to bring joy rather than grief.
why.b: Wrong. Proverbs 9:10 is quoted in Chapter 4 as a REQUIREMENT for wisdom, not as evidence of losing it.
why.c: Wrong. That is from Ecclesiastes 1:13-17, quoted in Chapter 8 as evidence that Solomon MEDITATED, which is a positive.
why.d: Wrong. Proverbs 3:13 is quoted under JOY as a product of wisdom.

prompt: According to the passage, what was the root cause of Solomon's fall?

options.text: He changed his God, and God turned His back on him
He grew proud of the temple he had built
He stopped meditating on the law
He trusted his own understanding instead of God's

explanation: Stated twice: 'When Solomon changed his God, God turned His back on him', and again at the end. His journey to changing his God began with losing his wisdom, and it was his wives who turned his heart after other gods.

why.a: Correct. Changing his God is named as the cause, and the phrase is repeated for emphasis.
why.b: Wrong. He built the tabernacle and dedicated it amid glory, which the passage treats as a good phase.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 8 praises Solomon's meditation without qualification.
why.d: Wrong. Self-trust destroyed AHITOPHEL, and pride is named as the devil's tool, but Solomon's stated cause is that he changed his God.

prompt: How many wives and concubines does the passage say Solomon had?

options.text: Seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines
Three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines
One thousand wives in all
Seventy wives and thirty concubines

explanation: From 1 Kings 11: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned away his heart.

why.a: Correct. Seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, in that order.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the obvious trap, since the two numbers are simply swapped.
why.c: Wrong. The total is right but the verse gives two distinct groups, and the distinction is what gets tested.
why.d: Wrong. Both figures are wrong by a factor of ten.

prompt: Which nations are named as the origin of the strange women Solomon loved?

options.text: Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians and Hittites, together with the daughter of Pharaoh
Canaanites, Perizzites, Jebusites and Amorites
Philistines, Assyrians and Babylonians
Chaldeans, Syrians and Egyptians

explanation: Five nations plus Pharaoh's daughter, all quoted from 1 Kings 11:1. God had said of these nations that they would surely turn away your heart after their gods.

why.a: Correct. These five, plus the daughter of Pharaoh who is named separately.
why.b: Wrong. A genuine biblical list of nations that does not appear in this passage.
why.c: Wrong. None of these three are named here.
why.d: Wrong. The Chaldeans belong to the Daniel material, and Egypt appears only via Pharaoh's daughter and Solomon's wisdom exceeding Egypt's.

prompt: How many times does the quoted passage say the LORD had appeared to Solomon?

options.text: Twice
Once
Three times
Seven times

explanation: 'the LORD God of Israel, which had appeared unto him twice'. It aggravates the offence: he had two direct encounters and still kept not that which the LORD commanded.

why.a: Correct. Twice, as the quoted verse states.
why.b: Wrong. Once would weaken the charge the verse is making.
why.c: Wrong. Three is not the number given.
why.d: Wrong. Seven appears nowhere in this passage.

prompt: Which two adversaries did God stir up against Solomon?

options.text: Hadad the Edomite and Rezon the son of Eliadah
Jeroboam and Rehoboam
Hadadezer and Absalom
Ahitophel and Absalom

explanation: Hadad the Edomite, of the king's seed in Edom, and Rezon the son of Eliadah, who fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah and reigned over Syria.

why.a: Correct. These two are named, from 1 Kings 11:14 and 11:23.
why.b: Wrong. Neither appears in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Hadadezer is mentioned, but as Rezon's former lord rather than as an adversary of Solomon.
why.d: Wrong. Ahitophel and Absalom belong to David's reign, and Ahitophel appears in this book as a separate warning about meekness.

prompt: What does the passage name as one of the devil's greatest tools of defilement?

options.text: Pride
Fear
Doubt
Idleness

explanation: Pride, described concretely: the moment things begin to work, the tendency is to kiss your palm in the secret and say 'No one else except me. If I were not there, would it have worked?'

why.a: Correct. Pride is named, and it is what destroyed Ahitophel and threatened Solomon.
why.b: Wrong. Fear is an enemy of INSPIRATION in Chapter 6 and a paralyser of mentality in Chapter 9.
why.c: Wrong. Doubt is not a category this book uses.
why.d: Wrong. Idleness appears in the Ecclesiastes 10:18 epigraph about the decaying building, not here.

prompt: How does the passage describe Ahitophel's standing in David's day, and his end?

options.text: Consulting him was like consulting the Almighty Himself, yet he lost his wisdom to self and pride and hung himself
He was distrusted from the beginning and died in obscurity
He served faithfully to the end of his life
He was replaced by a wiser counsellor and retired

explanation: The height makes the fall. The author adds that suicide is the height of madness, so at that moment Ahitophel was the most foolish human being on planet earth.

why.a: Correct. Both the height and the fall are given, and the cause is self and pride.
why.b: Wrong. He was trusted absolutely, which is the whole point.
why.c: Wrong. He went over to Absalom and then killed himself.
why.d: Wrong. His counsel was REJECTED once, and that single rejection is what he could not bear.

prompt: What has the author told God about blessing?

options.text: Don't bless me with what will become a curse in my hands, and whatever will make my head get bigger, don't let it reach my hand
Give me neither poverty nor riches
Give me only what I can manage without help
Withhold nothing, for I will use it all for You

explanation: He also asks God not to try him with what will hurt him, and to leave him where He thinks is safest. It follows the prayers that the wealth or position that would make you change your God may never reach you.

why.a: Correct. Both clauses are his, and the swollen head image is his own.
why.b: Wrong. That is Agur's prayer in Proverbs, which this book does not quote.
why.c: Wrong. Self-sufficiency is not the concern; safety from what would change his God is.
why.d: Wrong. This is nearly the opposite of what he prays.

topic: the spirit of a sound mind
prompt: Which scripture is quoted for God having given us the spirit of power, love and a sound mind?

options.text: 2 Timothy 1:7
1 Corinthians 2:16
Ephesians 4:23
Romans 8:6

explanation: 2 Timothy 1:6-7 and 14 are quoted together under Keep The Treasure, including the charge to keep that good thing by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.

why.a: Correct. 2 Timothy 1:7 is the power, love and sound mind verse.
why.b: Wrong. 1 Corinthians 2:16 is the mind of Christ, from Chapter 1.
why.c: Wrong. Ephesians 4:23 is being renewed in the spirit of your mind, also Chapter 1.
why.d: Wrong. Romans 8:6 is carnally minded is death.

prompt: With whom does the passage say the gift of a sound mind will not work?

options.text: The crooked, the perverse, the proud and the defiled
The idle, the fearful and the doubting
The poor, the untaught and the unwilling
The angry, the bitter and the unforgiving

explanation: Four kinds, and the positive counterpart is given at once: it will only be sustained by those who live in the fear of the Lord. Chapter 9 adds that no crooked man or woman is a worthy candidate for mental excellence.

why.a: Correct. These four are named, and they are all moral rather than circumstantial.
why.b: Wrong. Fear and idleness are treated elsewhere but are not this list.
why.c: Wrong. Poverty is never a disqualification in this book; it argues the opposite.
why.d: Wrong. Anger and bitterness are not categories the book uses.

prompt: What does the passage say it takes to earn dignity?

options.text: Integrity
Diligence
Patience
Humility

explanation: 'No crooked or perverse Christian has a future. It takes integrity to earn dignity.' Chapter 9 says the same the other way round: every man of integrity naturally enjoys mental dignity.

why.a: Correct. Integrity, and the rhyme with dignity is why the line is memorable.
why.b: Wrong. Diligence appears in 'Keep thy heart with all diligence', a different context.
why.c: Wrong. Patience appears only in the Hebrews 6:12 citation.
why.d: Wrong. Meekness is required to keep wisdom flowing, but the word paired with dignity here is integrity.

prompt: Whom does the passage list as having made it, in contrast to Solomon?

options.text: Joseph, Daniel, Apostle Paul and Jesus
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
Moses, Joshua and Caleb
David, Elijah and Elisha

explanation: 'Solomon started his journey as the wisest, but ended as the most foolish. Joseph made it! Daniel, Apostle Paul and Jesus made it! You are going to make it too!'

why.a: Correct. These four are named as having finished well.
why.b: Wrong. Isaac and Jacob appear as examples of inspiration in Chapter 6, not in this list.
why.c: Wrong. Moses appears for Jethro's counsel and for laying hands on Joshua, but not here.
why.d: Wrong. David is the meditation example, and Elijah and Elisha belong to quietness and singing.

prompt: How do the scriptures describe Jesus, according to this passage?

options.text: As the wisdom and power of God, having the Spirit without measure, declared the Son of God with power according to the spirit of holiness
As the author and finisher of our faith
As the firstborn among many brethren
As the express image of the Father's person

explanation: Three citations run together: 1 Corinthians 1:24, John 3:34 and Romans 1:4. He is offered as a successful carrier of divine wisdom throughout His time.

why.a: Correct. All three descriptions are given here with their citations.
why.b: Wrong. The book applies author and finisher to the FEAR OF THE LORD in Chapter 4, not to Jesus.
why.c: Wrong. A genuine phrase from Romans that this book does not quote.
why.d: Wrong. Another real description, from Hebrews, that does not appear here.

prompt: What does the passage say all Solomon's money could not restore to him?

options.text: His joy, peace and pleasantness
His kingdom and his throne
His reputation among the nations
His health and his years

explanation: Those three are precisely the products of divine wisdom listed earlier in the chapter, so losing wisdom means losing exactly what wisdom supplies.

why.a: Correct. Joy, peace and pleasantness, all three of which were named as products of wisdom.
why.b: Wrong. The kingdom's division is not discussed in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Reputation is not what the passage says he lost.
why.d: Wrong. Health and long life are products of wisdom in the chapter, but the three named here are joy, peace and pleasantness.

prompt: What does the passage say about one striking insight?

options.text: It is worth much more in value than a lifetime of struggles
It must be tested before it is trusted
It comes only after years of study
It should be shared quickly before it is forgotten

explanation: The line closes Chapter 5 and returns in Chapter 11, where one striking supernatural insight is said to be enough to release a man from prison and plant him in the palace.

why.a: Correct. Worth more than a lifetime of struggles, which is the book's summary of its own case.
why.b: Wrong. Testing insight is never discussed.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 6 says inspiration has nothing to do with a man's age, so time is not the price.
why.d: Wrong. Sharing is not the counsel attached to this line.

prompt: Fill the blank from Proverbs 3:18: "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that {{1}} her."
explanation: Retaineth. It is the word the whole section turns on, because retaining implies you can fail to retain, which is exactly what Solomon did. Findeth is the trap, because that is verse 13.

prompt: The passage says Ahitophel lost his wisdom because God found a wiser counsellor to replace him.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False. He lost his wisdom to self and pride. The trigger was that his counsel was rejected once, after years of being accepted as though it came from God, and he could not bear it.

why.true: Wrong. No replacement is mentioned, and the cause named is internal rather than external.
why.false: Correct. Self and pride are what he lost it to, which is why he appears under the discussion of pride as the devil's tool.

prompt: What does the passage say the wisdom treasure from above does for its carrier?

options.text: It glorifies its carrier, causing them to come out of obscurity into the limelight, so they emerge a natural star on the earth
It hides its carrier until the appointed time
It makes its carrier indifferent to recognition
It transfers to another when its carrier dies

explanation: Obscurity to limelight is a recurring pair in this book. Chapter 2 uses it of a business coming out of obscurity, and Chapter 4 says divine wisdom naturally announces its carrier.

why.a: Correct. Glorifying its carrier and moving them from obscurity into the limelight, ending as a natural star on the earth.
why.b: Wrong. Concealment is the opposite of what the book claims for wisdom.
why.c: Wrong. The book wants you to be the envy of your generation, not indifferent to it.
why.d: Wrong. Transfer at death is never suggested.
